newsitem.title: INDIA: Non-Aligned seek bigger, unbiased U.N. council.
newsitem.headline: Non-Aligned seek bigger, unbiased U.N. council.

text.p: Foreign ministers of more than 100 nations of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) said on Tuesday that the U.N. Security Council should not discriminate between rich and poor countries.

At the end of a two-day meeting panel also called for a special session of the U.N. General Assembly on the Middle East, which figured prominently at Monday's opening attended by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

"There shall be no partial or selective expansion or enlargement of the membership of the Security Council to the detriment of developing countries," the ministers said in a special declaration on U.N. reforms.
"Attempts to exclude NAM from any enlargement would be unacceptable to the movement," Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told a news conference after the meeting.

The ministers also sought to eliminate the veto power of the permanent members of the council -- the United States, Britain, France, China and Russia -- as part of the move to reform the United Nations.

An Indian diplomat said the wording was aimed at discouraging a pending proposal from the General Assembly president, Razali Ismail, that could see Japan and Germany included as permanent members in an expanded Security Council.
The proposal, made earlier this year in New York, aims to complete a restructuring of the council by next February.

The meeting of the 113-nation Non-Aligned Movement, widely considered irrelevant by critics after the end of the Cold War, received a boost from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who backed efforts for U.N. reforms in the inauguration he attended on Monday.
In a forceful address, Arafat attacked Israel for its recent attempts to build 6,500 homes in Palestinian territory captured in 1967, violating a Middle East peace accord.
Peace talks were halted after Israel began work last month on the new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, sparking daily clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops.
Responding to a call from Arafat, the ministers on Tuesday adopted a special declaration calling members to freeze ties at the current level with the Jewish state.
But officials said the nations were free to express their reservations over the move and were not bound to freeze ties.
The ministers adopted a 100-page document called the New Delhi Declaration that spoke for developing countries' interests on a number of economic, political and environmental concerns.

"The ministers called on the Conference on Disarmament to establish, on priority, an ad-hoc commitee to start negotiations on a phased programme for the complete elimination of nuclear weapons within a specific framework of time, including a Nuclear Weapons Convention," the declaration said.
The Conference on Disarmament is a Geneva-based forum for arms control negotiations.
"The use of the veto should be curtailed with a view to its eventual elimination," the declaration on U.N. reform said.

India, which has lobbied for a permanent seat on the Security Council, is among leading NAM members who feel its veto powers often put it in opposition to the General Assembly, where all members are equal.
The meeting elected South Africa to be the next host and chairman of NAM for a summit whose dates are yet to be announced.
It also adopted a separate declaration on environmental and economic issues, asking developed countries to boost aid to developing countries and transfer technologies to protect the environment.
